Call center agents and AI: easier for 40%, more stressful under monitoring

Artificial intelligence has entered call centers. It suggests answers to agents, summarizes conversations and analyzes calls. But how do the people who work with it every day perceive it? The answer depends heavily on how it is used.

A survey of 3,366 contact center agents in the United States, conducted between December 2022 and January 2023 and included in Statista's dossier on call centers, gives precise insights. AI appears both as a help and as a source of pressure, depending on how it is deployed.

A help when it serves the customer

When AI is used for customer information tasks, 40% of agents surveyed say it has made their work easier. And the majority believe it has improved the service delivered to customers in those situations.

In practice, these are tools that help the agent quickly find the right information, retrieve a customer's history or prepare a reply. The agent stays in control, and the tool saves time on tedious searches.

In that scenario, AI is seen as support. It improves the conversation with the customer without changing the nature of the job.

A source of stress when it monitors

The picture changes radically when AI is used to monitor agents' work. In the same survey, the majority of agents say AI makes their work more stressful when it is used to monitor their activity.

For training, more than 30% of agents also say AI makes work more stressful. And for feedback on their performance, the majority again see AI as a source of stress.

These results show that the problem is not the technology itself, but the intent behind its deployment. A tool that helps is welcomed; a tool that grades is endured.

Companies moving ahead without always knowing where

On the company side, the same dossier reports that about 46% of US companies surveyed said they used AI tools such as ChatGPT, virtual assistants or chatbots in their activities. 15% did not know whether such tools were used in their organization.

That last figure is telling. When one company in seven does not know whether it uses AI, it is unlikely to have thought carefully about how these tools affect its teams. Agents then risk enduring uses decided without them.

Agent experience and customer experience are linked

A stressed agent does not deliver a good customer experience. Constant monitoring pushes agents to hit indicators (call length, number of contacts handled) rather than truly solve the customer's problem. Customers feel it: shortened conversations, standardized answers, the impression of not being heard.

As we saw in another article, 38% of agents were not satisfied with their job according to a 2017 survey. Poorly used AI risks making that worse; well-used AI can improve it.

Agents also notice when a tool's figures are used against them rather than to help them. That perception alone can damage team morale, regardless of the tool's real accuracy.

Analyzing conversations to understand customers

There is another way to use conversation analysis: to understand customers, not to monitor agents. Automatic language analysis can read every transcribed call to identify why customers call, what frustrates them and which problems keep coming back unresolved.

That information helps fix the causes of difficult calls: a confusing procedure, information missing from the website, a recurring product defect. Fewer tense calls mean less pressure on agents and a better experience for customers. Our call centers page explains this approach.

The models used are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case; data stays hosted in France and is never used to train models.

The right questions before deploying a tool

Before introducing an AI tool into a contact center, a few simple questions help avoid pitfalls. What will it be used for first: helping the agent, understanding the customer or controlling activity? Were agents involved in the choice? Will results be shared with them, and for what purpose?

The answers often determine whether the tool will be experienced as help or as a constraint. The 2023 survey shows the difference is clear, and that it directly affects the quality of service customers receive.

A simple principle helps: share with agents the same insights you share with managers, and use them to remove obstacles rather than to rank people.
